_This page is generated from src/transcript.ts and src/harnesses/, so it says what the tool does._

Every adapter turns the stream of its harness into one ordered list of events. An event is the assistant's text, a tool call, or a tool result. Checks and graders read that list, and nothing else reads the raw stream. A check never needs to know which CLI wrote the events.

The tool calls in a run record are always taken from the transcript, so the two cannot disagree.

## Where it is written

The whole transcript is written to `<label><rep>.transcript.json`, next to the stream file, before any check runs. The file is pretty JSON and is never cut. The run record in `results.json` has `transcriptFile`: the path of that file, relative to the output directory. A run that could not be scored has `null`.

A `command` check gets the absolute path of the file in `SKILL_EVALS_TRANSCRIPT`.

```json
{
  "checks": [
    {
      "type": "command",
      "run": "grep -q 'npm test' \"$SKILL_EVALS_TRANSCRIPT\"",
      "timeoutSeconds": 30
    }
  ]
}
```

## The events

Each event has `index`, `turn` (null where the harness does not group calls; a tool result has the turn of its call), `userTurn`, `role`, `agent`, `type` and these fields where they apply:

- `callId` joins a tool call to its tool result.
- `kind`, `name` and `input` describe the call. A tool result takes the name and kind of its call.
- `output` is what the tool returned. `isError` is true when the harness marked the call as failed.
- `text` is what the assistant said.
- `bytes` is the size in UTF-8 of the `text` or `output` as decoded, before any cut.
- `durationMs` is how long a tool call took, where the stream says.

A case with a `history.json` keeps its seeded messages out of this file: the file holds the agent's events only, numbered from 0 as the reasons of the checks quote them. The messages are in `<label><rep>.history.json` next to it, as `history.json` has them, and a `command` check gets that path in `SKILL_EVALS_HISTORY` (not set for a case with no history). No check reads the history: `tool_called`, `tool_order`, the skill checks, `transcript_matches`, the output checks, `agent_dispatched` and `asked_user` see the agent's events only, and `rejudge` and `rescore` read the same files. The judge sees no history in this release, and its task text is the case's prompt without the block. `show` prints the agent's events at their own index and the history after a heading as `h0`, `h1` and so on, with each message's role. See [Multi-turn cases](../guides/multi-turn.md#start-from-a-conversation-that-already-happened).

Every event carries the agent that produced it: `agent` is `{ id, type, parent, depth }`, and the main thread is `{ "id": "main", "type": "main", "parent": null, "depth": 0 }`. Claude Code attributes child events: an event with a `parent_tool_use_id` belongs to the agent that the call of that id started, and it declares `childCalls` and `childText`. Every other adapter attributes every event to the main agent and declares neither capability, so a check with `by` is not applicable there. A call of kind `subagent` also records `dispatch`, `{ type, model, effort }`: what its input chose for the agent, each null where the stream does not show it (Claude Code reads `subagent_type`, `model` and `effort`; the other adapters show none). `agent_dispatched` reads it. Where the stream reports usage on each assistant message (Claude Code), the run record's `agentTokens` sums it by agent id, `main` or the id of the dispatch call; it is null elsewhere, and `tokens` stays the run's own total. A run record keeps `toolCalls` with their inputs and never their outputs.

## What each harness puts in it

| Captured                          | `pi` | `claude-code` | `cursor` | `opencode` | `codex` |
| --------------------------------- | ---- | ------------- | -------- | ---------- | ------- |
| Tool calls with their input       | yes  | yes           | yes      | yes        | yes     |
| Assistant text between tool calls | yes  | yes           | no       | yes        | yes     |
| Tool outputs                      | yes  | yes           | no       | yes        | yes     |
| Assistant turn on each event      | yes  | yes           | no       | yes        | no      |
| Tool duration                     | no   | no            | no       | yes        | no      |

An adapter declares a capability only when a parser test proves it on a fixture stream. `test/fixtures/README.md` says which fixtures were captured from a real CLI and which were written from the CLI's documentation. A check that needs a part that its harness lacks makes its case not applicable there. See [Capabilities](capabilities.md).

A tool matcher or a check on tool calls can bound a call's duration with `minDurationMs` and `maxDurationMs`. That needs `toolDurations`; a call whose duration is unknown never fits a bound.

A skill-tool call whose tool result was an error is not resolved, on a harness that has `toolOutputs`. Elsewhere the rule is the one it was.

## Checks that read it

`transcript_matches`, `transcript_lacks`, `tool_output_matches`, `tool_output_lacks` and `tool_output_size` read these events. They need `assistantText` or `toolOutputs`, as the table says. A pattern sees at most the first 1,000,000 characters of one event's text, input or output. See [Write a case](../guides/write-a-case.md#what-the-agent-said-and-what-its-tools-returned).

## Size and bad bytes

The copy of the transcript that is handed to a judge cuts any single `text` or `output` longer than 20,000 bytes. A cut event has `truncated: true` and keeps its original `bytes`. The file on disk is never cut.

The output of a harness is decoded as UTF-8 with replacement, so a tool that prints invalid bytes never makes a run fail. Each invalid byte sequence becomes one U+FFFD character, which is three bytes in UTF-8, so a truncated sequence such as `E2 82` is one replacement character. `bytes` counts the text as it was decoded, not the raw bytes the tool wrote.
